claim: Innate lymphoid cells (ILCs) represent the most recently identified subset of effector lymphocytes, with key roles in the orchestration of early immune responses.
source: Innate lymphoid cells (ILCs) represent the most recently identified subset of effector lymphocytes, with key roles in the orchestration of early immune responses.
evidence: This is a general statement about ILCs that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field of immunology.

claim: The role of ILCs in cancer remains poorly defined despite their established involvement in the pathogenesis of many inflammatory disorders.
source: Despite their established involvement in the pathogenesis of many inflammatory disorders, the role of ILCs in cancer remains poorly defined.
evidence: This statement acknowledges existing knowledge about ILCs in inflammatory disorders while identifying a gap in understanding their role in cancer.

claim: Among all ILC subsets, ILCPs elicited the strongest upregulation of adhesion molecules in endothelial cells (ECs) in vitro.
source: We show that, among all ILC subsets, ILCPs elicited the strongest upregulation of adhesion molecules in endothelial cells (ECs) in vitro
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from co-culture experiments shown in Figure 1b.

claim: ILCP-mediated EC activation occurs mainly in a contact-dependent manner.
source: We show that, among all ILC subsets, ILCPs elicited the strongest upregulation of adhesion molecules in endothelial cells (ECs) in vitro, mainly in a contact-dependent manner
evidence: This is supported by transwell experiments shown in Figure 2c demonstrating that physical separation prevents EC activation.

claim: ILCP-mediated EC activation occurs through tumor necrosis factor receptor- and RANK-dependent engagement of the NF-κB pathway.
source: We show that, among all ILC subsets, ILCPs elicited the strongest upregulation of adhesion molecules in endothelial cells (ECs) in vitro, mainly in a contact-dependent manner through the tumor necrosis factor receptor- and RANK-dependent engagement of the NF-κB pathway.
evidence: This is supported by blocking experiments with Fc fusion proteins (Figure 4) and NF-κB inhibition experiments (Figure 3a).

claim: The ILCP-mediated activation of ECs is functional by fostering the adhesion of other innate and adaptive immune cells.
source: Moreover, the ILCP-mediated activation of the ECs resulted to be functional by fostering the adhesion of other innate and adaptive immune cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by static adhesion assays shown in Figure 5 where various immune cell types adhered to ILCP-exposed ECs.

claim: Pre-exposure of ILCPs to human tumor cell lines strongly impaired their capacity to activate ECs.
source: Interestingly, pre-exposure of ILCPs to human tumor cell lines strongly impaired this capacity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6c where tumor cell pre-exposure reduced ILCP-mediated EC activation.

claim: Three main distinct subsets of non-NK helper-like ILCs have been described: ILC1s, ILC2s, and ILC3s.
source: Besides conventional natural killer (cNK) cells, three main distinct subsets of non-NK helper-like ILCs have been described so far, mirroring the transcriptional and functional phenotype of CD4+ T helper (Th) cell subsets (Diefenbach et al., 2014): ILC1s, ILC2s, and ILC3s
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Diefenbach et al., 2014.

claim: ILC1s, ILC2s, and ILC3s mainly produce IFN-γ, IL-4/IL-5/IL-13, and IL-17A/IL-22 respectively.
source: ILC1s, ILC2s, and ILC3s, that mainly produce IFN-γ, IL-4/IL-5/IL-13, and IL-17A/IL-22 respectively (Mjösberg and Spits, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mjösberg and Spits, 2016.

claim: A population of circulating Lin- CD127+CD117+CRTH2− ILCs, able to differentiate into all ILC subsets, has been identified in the periphery and named ILC precursors (ILCPs).
source: In human tissues, the majority of ILCs is mainly terminally differentiated, while a population of circulating Lin- CD127+CD117+CRTH2− ILCs, able to differentiate into all ILC subsets, has been recently identified in the periphery and named ILC precursors (ILCPs, Lim et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lim et al., 2017.

claim: ILCPs are characterized by the expression of CD62L that drives their migration to the lymph nodes.
source: ILCPs are characterized by the expression of CD62L that drives their migration to the lymph nodes (Bar-Ephraim et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bar-Ephraim et al., 2019.

claim: ILCs rely on IL-7 for their development.
source: Enriched at surface barriers, ILCs rely on IL-7 for their development and promptly respond to tissue- and cell-derived signals by producing effector cytokines in an antigen-independent manner (Nussbaum et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nussbaum et al., 2017.

claim: ILCs promptly respond to tissue- and cell-derived signals by producing effector cytokines in an antigen-independent manner.
source: Enriched at surface barriers, ILCs rely on IL-7 for their development and promptly respond to tissue- and cell-derived signals by producing effector cytokines in an antigen-independent manner (Nussbaum et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nussbaum et al., 2017.

claim: ILC subsets have important effector functions during the early stages of the immune response against microbes, in tissue repair and in the anatomical containment of commensals at surface barriers.
source: The different ILC subsets have important effector functions during the early stages of the immune response against microbes, in tissue repair and in the anatomical containment of commensals at surface barriers (Hazenberg and Spits, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hazenberg and Spits, 2014.

claim: ILCs have been shown to exert pro- and anti-tumoral activity by interacting with different cell types, including endothelial and stromal cells, depending on the ILC subset involved and tumor type.
source: In addition, depending on the ILC subset that is involved and on the tumor type (Salomé and Jandus, 2018; Chiossone et al., 2018; Ercolano et al., 2019; Ercolano et al., 2020), ILCs have been shown to also exert pro- and anti-tumoral activity by interacting with different cell types, including endothelial and stromal cells.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Salomé and Jandus, 2018; Chiossone et al., 2018; Ercolano et al., 2019; Ercolano et al., 2020).

claim: In a subcutaneous melanoma mouse model, IL-12-responsive NKp46+ ILCs recruited to the tumor supported massive leukocyte infiltration through upregulation of adhesion molecules in the tumor vasculature.
source: In a subcutaneous melanoma mouse model, IL-12-responsive NKp46+ ILCs, recruited to the tumor, supported a massive leukocyte infiltration through the upregulation of adhesion molecules in the tumor vasculature (Eisenring et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Eisenring et al., 2010.

claim: NKp44+ ILC3s were found to be present at early stage in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients.
source: In humans, NKp44+ ILC3s were found to be present at early stage in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients (Carrega et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Carrega et al., 2015.

claim: NKp44+ ILC3s correlate with a more favorable prognosis in NSCLC patients, possibly by promoting intratumoral tertiary lymphoid structure (TLS) formation.
source: In humans, NKp44+ ILC3s were found to be present at early stage in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients (Carrega et al., 2015) and to correlate with a more favorable prognosis, possibly by promoting intratumoral tertiary lymphoid structure (TLS) formation (Dieu-Nosjean et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Carrega et al., 2015 and Dieu-Nosjean et al., 2008.

claim: Scant data are available about the interaction between human ILCs and the vascular endothelium.
source: However, scant data are available about the interaction between human ILCs and the vascular endothelium, which constitutes the physical barrier to be crossed by peripheral blood (PB) immune cells to migrate into tissues where to exert their effector functions (Nourshargh et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in the literature, supported by citation to Nourshargh et al., 2010 for the role of endothelium.

claim: The vascular endothelium constitutes the physical barrier to be crossed by peripheral blood immune cells to migrate into tissues where they exert their effector functions.
source: However, scant data are available about the interaction between human ILCs and the vascular endothelium, which constitutes the physical barrier to be crossed by peripheral blood (PB) immune cells to migrate into tissues where to exert their effector functions (Nourshargh et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nourshargh et al., 2010.

claim: Human primed ILCPs can interact with endothelial cells and upregulate adhesion molecules.
source: In this study, we show for the first time that human primed ILCPs can interact with endothelial cells (ECs), upregulate adhesion molecules, and stimulate their pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Human primed ILCPs stimulate pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion in endothelial cells.
source: In this study, we show for the first time that human primed ILCPs can interact with endothelial cells (ECs), upregulate adhesion molecules, and stimulate their pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: ILCP-mediated EC activation occurs through NF-κB, primarily in a contact-dependent manner that engages surface TNF and RANKL.
source: This activation occurs through NF-κB, primarily in a contact-dependent manner that engages surface TNF and RANKL.
evidence: This is supported by NF-κB inhibition experiments (Figure 3a), transwell experiments (Figure 2c), and blocking experiments (Figure 4).

claim: The ILCP-mediated activation of ECs allows the adhesion of freshly isolated PB immune cells.
source: We report that the ILCP-mediated activation of the ECs is functional, i.e., it allows the adhesion of freshly isolated PB immune cells.
evidence: This is supported by static adhesion assay data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The ability of ILCPs to activate ECs is dampened after co-culture with tumor cells.
source: Moreover, we show that the ability of ILCPs to activate ECs is dampened after the co-culture with tumor cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6c.

claim: ILCPs were the only subset that significantly upregulated E-Selectin, ICAM-1, and VCAM-1 on the EC surface, compared to ILC1s and ILC2s.
source: Upon exposure of ECs to in vitro-expanded ILC subsets, ILCPs were the only subset that significantly upregulated the adhesion molecules E-Selectin, ICAM-1, and VCAM-1 on the EC surface, if compared to ILC1s and ILC2s (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is directly supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: In vitro-expanded ILCPs can activate primary human dermal blood ECs (HDBECs).
source: We confirmed the ability of in vitro-expanded ILCPs to activate ECs using other primary human dermal blood ECs, i.e., HDBECs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Following in vitro expansion, ILCPs upregulated NKp44 and CD69 compared to their ex vivo counterparts.
source: Following in vitro expansion, we observed that ILCPs upregulated NKp44 and CD69 as well as CD45RO and RORγt, if compared to their ex vivo counterparts, while maintaining similar levels of expression of NKp46 and CD62L (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c and d)
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c and d.

claim: Following in vitro expansion, ILCPs upregulated CD45RO and RORγt compared to their ex vivo counterparts.
source: Following in vitro expansion, we observed that ILCPs upregulated NKp44 and CD69 as well as CD45RO and RORγt, if compared to their ex vivo counterparts, while maintaining similar levels of expression of NKp46 and CD62L (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c and d)
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c and d.

claim: In vitro-expanded ILCPs maintained similar levels of expression of NKp46 and CD62L compared to their ex vivo counterparts.
source: Following in vitro expansion, we observed that ILCPs upregulated NKp44 and CD69 as well as CD45RO and RORγt, if compared to their ex vivo counterparts, while maintaining similar levels of expression of NKp46 and CD62L (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c and d)
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c and d.

claim: The in vitro expansion process conferred a more committed phenotype to ILCPs.
source: Following in vitro expansion, we observed that ILCPs upregulated NKp44 and CD69 as well as CD45RO and RORγt, if compared to their ex vivo counterparts, while maintaining similar levels of expression of NKp46 and CD62L (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c and d), suggesting that the in vitro expansion process conferred a more committed phenotype to this ILC subset.
evidence: This is inferred from the phenotypic changes observed in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c and d.

claim: No difference in T-bet or GATA3 expression in RORγt+ vs RORγt- ILCPs was observed.
source: Interestingly, no difference in T-bet or GATA3 expression in RORγt+ vs RORγt- cells was observed (Figure 1—figure supplement 1e), indicating that the expression or not of RORγt is not directly involved in the EC-activating capacity of ILCPs.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1e.

claim: The expression of RORγt is not directly involved in the EC-activating capacity of ILCPs.
source: Interestingly, no difference in T-bet or GATA3 expression in RORγt+ vs RORγt- cells was observed (Figure 1—figure supplement 1e), indicating that the expression or not of RORγt is not directly involved in the EC-activating capacity of ILCPs.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of difference in T-bet or GATA3 expression between RORγt+ and RORγt- ILCPs.

claim: Around 60% of in vitro-expanded ILCPs acquired NKp44 expression.
source: Since we observed that around 60% of in vitro-expanded ILCPs acquired NKp44 expression, we investigated the ability of NKp44+ vs NKp44- ILCPs to activate ECs.
evidence: This is based on observation from flow cytometry data.

claim: No significant difference was observed in the EC-activating capacity of NKp44+ vs NKp44- ILCPs.
source: As shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1f, no significant difference was observed in the EC-activating capacity of these two subpopulations, suggesting that the EC-activating capacity of ILCPs does not depend on the expression of NKp44.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1f.

claim: The EC-activating capacity of ILCPs does not depend on the expression of NKp44.
source: As shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1f, no significant difference was observed in the EC-activating capacity of these two subpopulations, suggesting that the EC-activating capacity of ILCPs does not depend on the expression of NKp44.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of difference in EC activation between NKp44+ and NKp44- ILCPs.

claim: In vitro-expanded ILCPs upregulated the expression of the chemokine receptors CCR6 and CXCR5 compared to their ex vivo counterparts.
source: Moreover, we observed that in vitro-expanded ILCPs upregulated the expression of the chemokine receptors CCR6 and CXCR5, i.e., two known LTi-like cells markers, compared to their ex vivo counterparts.
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c and d.

claim: CCR6 and CXCR5 are two known LTi-like cell markers.
source: Moreover, we observed that in vitro-expanded ILCPs upregulated the expression of the chemokine receptors CCR6 and CXCR5, i.e., two known LTi-like cells markers, compared to their ex vivo counterparts.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about LTi-like cell markers.

claim: Neuropilin1 (NRP1) was not expressed by circulating ILC3s.
source: Consistent with previous reports, Neuropilin1 (NRP1) was not expressed by circulating ILC3s (Shikhagaie et al., 2017) and was not upregulated after in vitro expansion.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Shikhagaie et al., 2017 and flow cytometry data.

claim: NRP1 was not upregulated in ILCPs after in vitro expansion.
source: Consistent with previous reports, Neuropilin1 (NRP1) was not expressed by circulating ILC3s (Shikhagaie et al., 2017) and was not upregulated after in vitro expansion.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c and d.

claim: In vitro-expanded ILCPs downregulated the expression of CD28 compared to ex vivo ILCPs.
source: Compared to ex vivo ILCPs, in vitro-expanded ILCPs downregulated the expression of CD28, although only 20% of circulating ILCPs expressed it (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c and d).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c and d.

claim: Only 20% of circulating ILCPs expressed CD28.
source: Compared to ex vivo ILCPs, in vitro-expanded ILCPs downregulated the expression of CD28, although only 20% of circulating ILCPs expressed it (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c and d).
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c and d.

claim: In vitro-expanded ILCPs acquire an activated phenotype in vitro.
source: Overall, these data suggest that not only in vitro-expanded ILCPs acquire an activated phenotype in vitro, but are also skewed toward an ILC3-like phenotype and share some phenotypical markers with LTi-like cells, while maintaining multipotent features as shown by the expression of T-bet and GATA3.
evidence: This is inferred from the upregulation of activation markers like CD69 and NKp44 shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c and d.

claim: In vitro-expanded ILCPs are skewed toward an ILC3-like phenotype.
source: Overall, these data suggest that not only in vitro-expanded ILCPs acquire an activated phenotype in vitro, but are also skewed toward an ILC3-like phenotype and share some phenotypical markers with LTi-like cells, while maintaining multipotent features as shown by the expression of T-bet and GATA3.
evidence: This is inferred from the upregulation of RORγt and ILC3-associated markers shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c and d.

claim: In vitro-expanded ILCPs share some phenotypical markers with LTi-like cells.
source: Overall, these data suggest that not only in vitro-expanded ILCPs acquire an activated phenotype in vitro, but are also skewed toward an ILC3-like phenotype and share some phenotypical markers with LTi-like cells, while maintaining multipotent features as shown by the expression of T-bet and GATA3.
evidence: This is inferred from the expression of CCR6 and CXCR5 shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c and d.

claim: In vitro-expanded ILCPs maintain multipotent features as shown by the expression of T-bet and GATA3.
source: Overall, these data suggest that not only in vitro-expanded ILCPs acquire an activated phenotype in vitro, but are also skewed toward an ILC3-like phenotype and share some phenotypical markers with LTi-like cells, while maintaining multipotent features as shown by the expression of T-bet and GATA3.
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry data showing T-bet and GATA3 expression in Figure 1—figure supplement 1e.

claim: None of the ex vivo-sorted ILC subsets could induce a significant activation of ECs.
source: As shown in Figure 1c, none of the isolated ILC subsets could induce a significant activation of ECs, suggesting that the EC-activating capacity of ILCPs is acquired during the in vitro expansion process.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: The EC-activating capacity of ILCPs is acquired during the in vitro expansion process.
source: As shown in Figure 1c, none of the isolated ILC subsets could induce a significant activation of ECs, suggesting that the EC-activating capacity of ILCPs is acquired during the in vitro expansion process.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison between ex vivo and in vitro-expanded ILCPs shown in Figures 1b and 1c.

claim: ILCPs were expanded in the presence of feeder cells, PHA, and IL-2.
source: Since ILCPs were expanded in the presence of feeder cells, PHA, and IL-2, it is conceivable that feeder-derived cytokines such as IL-12 and IL-1β are involved in the priming.
evidence: This is stated as part of the experimental methodology.

claim: Feeder-derived cytokines such as IL-12 and IL-1β are conceivably involved in the priming of ILCPs.
source: Since ILCPs were expanded in the presence of feeder cells, PHA, and IL-2, it is conceivable that feeder-derived cytokines such as IL-12 and IL-1β are involved in the priming.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the culture conditions and known cytokine production by feeder cells.

claim: Except for a statistically significant Th1-mediated upregulation of VCAM-1, all Th subsets failed to upregulate adhesion molecule expression on the EC surface.
source: As reported in the Figure 1—figure supplement 2b, except for a statistically significant Th1-mediated upregulation of VCAM-1, still not to the same extent as the ILCP-mediated induction, all Th subsets failed to upregulate adhesion molecule expression on the EC surface.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2b.

claim: Th1-mediated upregulation of VCAM-1 was not to the same extent as the ILCP-mediated induction.
source: As reported in the Figure 1—figure supplement 2b, except for a statistically significant Th1-mediated upregulation of VCAM-1, still not to the same extent as the ILCP-mediated induction, all Th subsets failed to upregulate adhesion molecule expression on the EC surface.
evidence: This is based on comparison of data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2b.

claim: In vitro-expanded ILCPs acquire the ability to interact with ECs by mediating the upregulation of adhesion molecule expression on the EC surface.
source: Overall, these data suggest that in vitro-expanded ILCPs not only acquire a more activated/ILC3-like phenotype in vitro, but also the ability of interacting with ECs by means of mediating the upregulation of adhesion molecule expression on the EC surface.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data showing phenotypic changes and functional capacity of in vitro-expanded ILCPs.

claim: Inflammation triggers the upregulation of adhesion molecules in ECs, promoting the accumulation of leukocytes and their adhesion to the blood vessel walls.
source: Inflammation triggers the upregulation of adhesion molecules in ECs, promoting the accumulation of leukocytes and their adhesion to the blood vessel walls.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field of vascular biology.

claim: Pro-inflammatory mediators such as TNF and IL-1β mediate the upregulation of adhesion molecules in ECs during inflammation.
source: This phenomenon is mediated by pro-inflammatory mediators, such as TNF and IL-1β (Collins et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Collins et al., 1995.

claim: Significantly higher levels of IL-6, IL-8, GM-CSF, and IFN-γ were observed in supernatants from EC/ILCP co-cultures.
source: As a consequence, to discriminate whether the EC activation by ILCPs was due to contact-dependent or soluble factor(s)-dependent mechanism(s), supernatants from the EC/ILCP co-cultures were analyzed. Significantly higher levels of IL-6, IL-8, GM-CSF, and IFN-γ were observed (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is supported by cytokine measurement data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: High levels of IL-6 and IL-8 transcripts were found in ECs exposed to ILCPs.
source: As reported in Figure 2b, high levels of IL-6 and IL-8 transcripts were found in ECs exposed to ILCPs, whereas TNF transcripts were high only in steady-state ILCPs
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: TNF transcripts were high only in steady-state ILCPs.
source: As reported in Figure 2b, high levels of IL-6 and IL-8 transcripts were found in ECs exposed to ILCPs, whereas TNF transcripts were high only in steady-state ILCPs
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: IL-6 and IL-8 measured in the supernatant derive from ECs.
source: As reported in Figure 2b, high levels of IL-6 and IL-8 transcripts were found in ECs exposed to ILCPs, whereas TNF transcripts were high only in steady-state ILCPs, indicating that IL-6 and IL-8 measured in the supernatant (Figure 2a) derive from ECs, and TNF from ILCPs.
evidence: This is inferred from qPCR data showing high IL-6 and IL-8 transcripts in ECs (Figure 2b).

claim: TNF measured in the supernatant derives from ILCPs.
source: As reported in Figure 2b, high levels of IL-6 and IL-8 transcripts were found in ECs exposed to ILCPs, whereas TNF transcripts were high only in steady-state ILCPs, indicating that IL-6 and IL-8 measured in the supernatant (Figure 2a) derive from ECs, and TNF from ILCPs.
evidence: This is inferred from qPCR data showing high TNF transcripts in ILCPs (Figure 2b).

claim: GM-CSF and IFN-γ transcripts were observed in both ECs and ILCPs before and after co-culture.
source: GM-CSF and IFN-γ transcripts were observed in both ECs and ILCPs before and after co-culture, indicating that both cell types contribute to the accumulation of these two cytokines in the supernatant.
evidence: This is based on qPCR data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Both ECs and ILCPs contribute to the accumulation of GM-CSF and IFN-γ in the supernatant.
source: GM-CSF and IFN-γ transcripts were observed in both ECs and ILCPs before and after co-culture, indicating that both cell types contribute to the accumulation of these two cytokines in the supernatant.
evidence: This is inferred from qPCR data showing transcripts in both cell types (Figure 2b).

claim: ILCPs failed to induce the expression of adhesion molecules on EC surface when cultured in transwell chambers with 0.4 μm pore.
source: To experimentally verify if the upregulation of adhesion molecules in ECs was dependent on these soluble factors, 0.4 μm pore transwell chambers were employed, to allow cytokine exchange between the two compartments yet avoiding the cell contact. In this context, ILCPs failed to induce the expression of adhesion molecules on EC surface (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The production of pro-inflammatory cytokines was dramatically reduced in the presence of the transwell insert.
source: Of note, the production of the pro-inflammatory cytokines was dramatically reduced in the presence of the transwell insert (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by cytokine measurement data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Cell-free supernatant from EC–ILCP co-culture did not lead to the upregulation of E-Selectin and VCAM-1 in ECs.
source: As reported in Figure 2d, cell-free supernatant did not lead to the upregulation of the adhesion molecules E-Selectin and VCAM-1 in ECs
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: ICAM-1 levels were found to be significantly increased when ECs were exposed to cell-free supernatant from EC–ILCP co-culture, compared to unstimulated ECs.
source: As reported in Figure 2d, cell-free supernatant did not lead to the upregulation of the adhesion molecules E-Selectin and VCAM-1 in ECs, although ICAM-1 levels were found to be significantly increased if compared to unstimulated ECs, yet not to the same extent as for ILCP-exposed ECs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: ICAM-1 upregulation by cell-free supernatant was not to the same extent as for ILCP-exposed ECs.
source: As reported in Figure 2d, cell-free supernatant did not lead to the upregulation of the adhesion molecules E-Selectin and VCAM-1 in ECs, although ICAM-1 levels were found to be significantly increased if compared to unstimulated ECs, yet not to the same extent as for ILCP-exposed ECs.
evidence: This is based on comparison of data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: No difference in terms of secretion of IL-6, IL-8, TNF, GM-CSF, and IFN-γ was observed between ex vivo- and in vitro-expanded ILCPs.
source: Finally, we analyzed the production of IL-6, IL-8, TNF, GM-CSF, and IFN-γ by ex vivo- and in vitro-expanded ILCPs. As shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b, no difference in terms of secretion of the indicated cytokines was observed.
evidence: This is supported by cytokine measurement data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Incubation of ECs with cell-free supernatant collected from pure ILCPs at the end of in vitro expansion did not provoke upregulation of adhesion molecules on EC surface.
source: Indeed, incubation of ECs during 3 hr with cell-free supernatant collected from pure ILCPs at the end of the in vitro expansion did not provoke upregulation of adhesion molecules on EC surface (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1c.

claim: ILCPs are superior to other ILC subsets in inducing the upregulation of adhesion molecules on ECs.
source: Overall, these data suggest that ILCPs are superior to other ILC subsets in inducing the upregulation of adhesion molecules on ECs and can also favor the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines, primarily in a contact-dependent manner.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparative data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: ILCPs can favor the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines, primarily in a contact-dependent manner.
source: Overall, these data suggest that ILCPs are superior to other ILC subsets in inducing the upregulation of adhesion molecules on ECs and can also favor the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines, primarily in a contact-dependent manner.
evidence: This is inferred from transwell and supernatant experiments shown in Figures 2c and 2d.

claim: Adhesion molecule expression can be induced in ECs during inflammatory responses by the activation of the NF-κB pathway.
source: It has been shown that adhesion molecule expression can be induced in ECs during inflammatory responses by the activation of different signaling pathways, among which the NF-κB pathway (Rahman and Fazal, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rahman and Fazal, 2011.

claim: ILCPs failed to significantly induce the expression of adhesion molecules on ECs pre-treated with IκB kinase (IKK) complex inhibitor (BAY 11–7082).
source: To test whether the induction of adhesion molecules by ILCPs was dependent on NF-κB, ECs were pre-treated during 1 hr with a IκB kinase (IKK) complex inhibitor (BAY 11–7082, Mori et al., 2002) to specifically prevent NF-κB activation. In this context, ILCPs failed to significantly induce the expression of adhesion molecules on pre-treated ECs (Figure 3a)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: ILCPs need to engage the NF-κB pathway to activate ECs in vitro.
source: In this context, ILCPs failed to significantly induce the expression of adhesion molecules on pre-treated ECs (Figure 3a), indicating that ILCPs need to engage the NF-κB pathway to activate ECs in vitro.
evidence: This is inferred from the NF-κB inhibition experiment shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The prevention of NF-κB activation in ECs led to a significant decrease of IL-6, as well as reduction in IL-8, GM-CSF, and IFN-γ secretion.
source: Similar to what we observed in the context of ILCPs cultured with ECs in the presence of a transwell insert, the prevention of NF-κB activation in ECs led to a significant decrease of IL-6, as well as reduction in IL-8, GM-CSF, and IFN-γ secretion (Figure 2—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is supported by cytokine measurement data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1d.

claim: Untreated ECs constitutively expressed the lymphotoxin-β receptor (LT-βR), as well as the tumor necrosis factor (TNF) receptors 1 and 2 (TNFR-1 and TNFR-2).
source: On one side, we observed that untreated ECs constitutively expressed the lymphotoxin-β receptor (LT-βR), as well as the tumor necrosis factor (TNF) receptors 1 and 2 (TNFR-1 and TNFR-2, respectively), whereas B-cell activating factor receptor (BAFF-R), CD40, and RANK were expressed only at low levels (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: BAFF-R, CD40, and RANK were expressed only at low levels on untreated ECs.
source: On one side, we observed that untreated ECs constitutively expressed the lymphotoxin-β receptor (LT-βR), as well as the tumor necrosis factor (TNF) receptors 1 and 2 (TNFR-1 and TNFR-2, respectively), whereas B-cell activating factor receptor (BAFF-R), CD40, and RANK were expressed only at low levels (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Following stimulation with TNF, CD30 expression became detectable on ECs.
source: Following stimulation with TNF, CD30 expression became detectable and BAFF-R and RANK expression increased, while CD40 and LT-βR expression remained unchanged (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Following stimulation with TNF, BAFF-R and RANK expression increased on ECs.
source: Following stimulation with TNF, CD30 expression became detectable and BAFF-R and RANK expression increased, while CD40 and LT-βR expression remained unchanged (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Following stimulation with TNF, CD40 and LT-βR expression remained unchanged on ECs.
source: Following stimulation with TNF, CD30 expression became detectable and BAFF-R and RANK expression increased, while CD40 and LT-βR expression remained unchanged (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Ex vivo ILCPs expressed high levels of the transmembrane form of lymphotoxin (LTα1β2) compared to in vitro-expanded ILCPs.
source: On the other side, when looking at extracellular NF-κB activating ligands on ex vivo ILCPs, we observed that they expressed high levels of the transmembrane form of lymphotoxin (LTα1β2), a described ligand for LT-βR (Madge et al., 2008), if compared to in vitro-expanded ILCPs (Figure 3c and d).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3c and d.

claim: LTα1β2 is a described ligand for LT-βR.
source: On the other side, when looking at extracellular NF-κB activating ligands on ex vivo ILCPs, we observed that they expressed high levels of the transmembrane form of lymphotoxin (LTα1β2), a described ligand for LT-βR (Madge et al., 2008), if compared to in vitro-expanded ILCPs (Figure 3c and d).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Madge et al., 2008.

claim: Both BAFF and CD30L were undetectable on ex vivo ILCPs.
source: Both BAFF and CD30L were undetectable and low levels of CD40L and RANKL were observed.
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3c and d.

claim: Low levels of CD40L and RANKL were observed on ex vivo ILCPs.
source: Both BAFF and CD30L were undetectable and low levels of CD40L and RANKL were observed.
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3c and d.

claim: In vitro-expanded ILCPs upregulated the expression of RANKL.
source: In contrast, in vitro-expanded ILCPs upregulated the expression of RANKL and downregulated that of LTα1β2 (Figure 3c and d).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3c and d.

claim: In vitro-expanded ILCPs downregulated the expression of LTα1β2.
source: In contrast, in vitro-expanded ILCPs upregulated the expression of RANKL and downregulated that of LTα1β2 (Figure 3c and d).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3c and d.

claim: Pro-inflammatory cytokines such as interleukin 12 (IL-12) can induce RANKL on human periodontal ligament cells in vitro.
source: It has been reported that pro-inflammatory cytokines, such as interleukin 12 (IL-12), can induce RANKL on human periodontal ligament cells in vitro (Issaranggun Na Ayuthaya et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Issaranggun Na Ayuthaya et al., 2017.

claim: After 24 hr stimulation of freshly ex vivo isolated ILCPs with IL-1β, increased expression of RANKL was observed compared to untreated ILCPs.
source: Surprisingly, after 24 hr stimulation of freshly ex vivo isolated ILCPs with IL-1β (Figure 3e), but not with IL-12 (data not shown), we observed increased expression of RANKL compared to untreated ILCPs.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3e.

claim: After 24 hr stimulation of freshly ex vivo isolated ILCPs with IL-12, no increased expression of RANKL was observed.
source: Surprisingly, after 24 hr stimulation of freshly ex vivo isolated ILCPs with IL-1β (Figure 3e), but not with IL-12 (data not shown), we observed increased expression of RANKL compared to untreated ILCPs.
evidence: This is stated based on experimental observation (data not shown).

claim: At the end of the in vitro expansion, ILCPs showed higher levels of TNF transcripts compared to ex vivo ILCPs.
source: However, at the end of the in vitro expansion, ILCPs showed higher levels of TNF transcripts compared to ex vivo ILCPs (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated based on experimental observation (data not shown).

claim: In vitro-expanded ILCPs express TNF, possibly present on the ILCP surface, to interact with ECs via TNFRs.
source: Overall, these data show that in vitro-expanded ILCPs express TNF, possibly present on the ILCP surface, to in vitro interact with ECs via TNFRs and upregulate RANKL expression, possibly via feeder-cell-derived IL-1β, to engage RANK on ECs.
evidence: This is inferred from TNF transcript data and blocking experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: In vitro-expanded ILCPs upregulate RANKL expression, possibly via feeder-cell-derived IL-1β, to engage RANK on ECs.
source: Overall, these data show that in vitro-expanded ILCPs express TNF, possibly present on the ILCP surface, to in vitro interact with ECs via TNFRs and upregulate RANKL expression, possibly via feeder-cell-derived IL-1β, to engage RANK on ECs.
evidence: This is inferred from RANKL upregulation data (Figure 3c-e) and IL-1β stimulation experiments (Figure 3e).

claim: ILCPs were still able to activate ECs in the presence of RANK:Fc blocking, with yet an inhibition of E-Selectin triggering in ECs.
source: Although ILCPs were still able to activate ECs in this setting with yet an inhibition of E-Selectin triggering in ECs (Figure 4a)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: The levels of IL-6 and GM-CSF were dramatically reduced when RANK:Fc was used to block RANK/RANKL interaction, compared to the cytokine composition of ECs cultured with steady-state ILCPs.
source: Although ILCPs were still able to activate ECs in this setting with yet an inhibition of E-Selectin triggering in ECs (Figure 4a), we observed that the levels of IL-6 and GM-CSF were dramatically reduced, if compared to the cytokine composition of ECs cultured with steady-state ILCPs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is supported by cytokine measurement data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1c.

claim: The EC expression of adhesion molecules was significantly reduced when ILCPs were pre-incubated with TNFR1:Fc and/or TNFR2:Fc.
source: Thus, we pre-incubated ILCPs in the presence of TNFR1:Fc and/or TNFR2:Fc and we observed that the EC expression of adhesion molecules was significantly reduced (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Inhibition with TNFR2:Fc was slightly more efficient than with TNFR1:Fc in reducing EC adhesion molecule expression.
source: In all cases, inhibition with TNFR2:Fc was slightly more efficient than with TNFR1:Fc, which could be explained by the greater affinity of TNFR2 for TNF (Grell et al., 1995).
evidence: This is based on comparison of data in Figure 4b and supported by citation to Grell et al., 1995.

claim: TNFR2 has greater affinity for TNF than TNFR1.
source: In all cases, inhibition with TNFR2:Fc was slightly more efficient than with TNFR1:Fc, which could be explained by the greater affinity of TNFR2 for TNF (Grell et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Grell et al., 1995.

claim: No difference in the cytokine secreted levels was observed when interfering with the TNF-TNFR signaling.
source: Of note, no difference in the cytokine secreted levels was observed (Figure 4—figure supplement 1d), suggesting that interfering with the TNF-TNFR signaling does not impact cytokine production in both cell types.
evidence: This is supported by cytokine measurement data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1d.

claim: Interfering with the TNF-TNFR signaling does not impact cytokine production in both ECs and ILCPs.
source: Of note, no difference in the cytokine secreted levels was observed (Figure 4—figure supplement 1d), suggesting that interfering with the TNF-TNFR signaling does not impact cytokine production in both cell types.
evidence: This is inferred from cytokine data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1d.

claim: Addition of RANK:Fc to TNFR1:Fc and TNFR2:Fc further slightly reduced E-Selectin, ICAM-1 and VCAM-1 levels, although the contribution of RANK:Fc was not significant.
source: Addition of RANK:Fc to TNFR1:Fc and TNFR2:Fc further slightly reduced E-Selectin, ICAM-1 and VCAM-1 levels, although the contribution of RANK:Fc was not significant (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: A decreased production of IL-6, IL-8, TNF, and GM-CSF was observed when blocking ligands of TNFR1, TNFR2, and RANK in ILCPs/ECs co-cultures.
source: However, we could observe a decreased production of the pro-inflammatory cytokine IL-6, IL-8, TNF, and GM-CSF (Figure 4—figure supplement 1e) when blocking ligands of TNFR1, TNFR2, and RANK in ILCPs/ECs co-cultures.
evidence: This is supported by cytokine measurement data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1e.

claim: ILCPs activate EC primarily through the engagement of TNFRs to upregulate adhesion molecules expression on EC surface.
source: Taken together, our data suggest that ILCPs activate EC primarily through the engagement of TNFRs to upregulate adhesion molecules expression on EC surface.
evidence: This is inferred from blocking experiments shown in Figure 4b and c.

claim: The engagement of RANK in ECs does not seem to have an additive effect in inducing adhesion molecules expression.
source: The engagement of RANK in ECs does not seem to have an additive effect in inducing adhesion molecules expression, but might act in synergy with tm-TNF to control the cytokine secretion and further support the EC activation.
evidence: This is inferred from the non-significant contribution of RANK:Fc in Figure 4c but decreased cytokines in Figure 4—figure supplement 1e.

claim: The engagement of RANK might act in synergy with tm-TNF to control the cytokine secretion and further support the EC activation.
source: The engagement of RANK in ECs does not seem to have an additive effect in inducing adhesion molecules expression, but might act in synergy with tm-TNF to control the cytokine secretion and further support the EC activation.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the combined blocking experiments shown in Figure 4c and Figure 4—figure supplement 1e.

claim: Following the 3 hr co-cultures, CD31+ ECs were isolated by FACS to remove adherent ILCPs and re-plated for static adhesion assay.
source: Briefly, following the 3 hr co-cultures, CD31+ ECs were isolated by FACS, to remove adherent ILCPs, and re-plated.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used.

claim: After FACS sorting, untreated ECs did not upregulate adhesion molecule expression on their cell surface.
source: After the sorting, untreated ECs (negative control) did not upregulate adhesion molecule expression on their cell surface, and ILCP-exposed ECs maintained comparable surface levels of adhesion molecule as before the FACS isolation procedure, showing that the sorting procedure did not affect the activation state of ECs in any of the conditions (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: ILCP-exposed ECs maintained comparable surface levels of adhesion molecule as before the FACS isolation procedure.
source: After the sorting, untreated ECs (negative control) did not upregulate adhesion molecule expression on their cell surface, and ILCP-exposed ECs maintained comparable surface levels of adhesion molecule as before the FACS isolation procedure, showing that the sorting procedure did not affect the activation state of ECs in any of the conditions (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: The FACS sorting procedure did not affect the activation state of ECs.
source: After the sorting, untreated ECs (negative control) did not upregulate adhesion molecule expression on their cell surface, and ILCP-exposed ECs maintained comparable surface levels of adhesion molecule as before the FACS isolation procedure, showing that the sorting procedure did not affect the activation state of ECs in any of the conditions (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of adhesion molecule levels before and after sorting shown in Figure 5a.

claim: ECs pre-exposed to ILCPs led to the adhesion of a significantly higher number of freshly isolated PBMCs compared to unstimulated ECs.
source: Interestingly, ECs pre-exposed to ILCPs led to the adhesion of a significantly higher number of freshly isolated PBMCs compared to unstimulated ECs.
evidence: This is supported by static adhesion assay data shown in Figure 5b and c.

claim: The ILCP modification of EC allowed a strong adhesion of T, B as well as NK cells and monocytes.
source: As shown in Figure 5b and c, the ILCP modification of EC allowed a strong adhesion of T, B as well as NK cells and monocytes.
evidence: This is supported by static adhesion assay data shown in Figure 5b and c.

claim: The inhibition of NF-κB activation prior stimulation with TNF strongly reduced the numbers of adhered T, B, NK cells, and monocytes.
source: As shown in Figure 5d, the inhibition of NF-κB activation prior stimulation with TNF strongly reduced the numbers of adhered T, B, NK cells, and monocytes.
evidence: This is supported by static adhesion assay data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: ILCs themselves could adhere to TNF-treated ECs.
source: In this setting, we could also observe that ILCs themselves could adhere to TNF-treated ECs (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is supported by static adhesion assay data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: A trend for a reduction in the number of adhered PBMCs to ECs was observed when NF-κB activation was prevented in ECs 30 min before performing the static adhesion assay, although not significant.
source: Interestingly, a trend for a reduction in the number of adhered PBMCs to ECs was also observed when NF-κB activation was prevented in ECs 30 min before performing the static adhesion assay (Figure 5d) although not significant.
evidence: This is based on static adhesion assay data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: The adhesion molecule expression induced by the ILCPs is functional and supports the adhesion of other immune cell types to ECs in vitro.
source: Overall, these data suggest that the adhesion molecule expression induced by the ILCPs is functional, i.e., it supports the adhesion of other immune cell types to ECs in vitro and relies on NF-κB activation.
evidence: This is inferred from static adhesion assay data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The adhesion of immune cells to ILCP-activated ECs relies on NF-κB activation.
source: Overall, these data suggest that the adhesion molecule expression induced by the ILCPs is functional, i.e., it supports the adhesion of other immune cell types to ECs in vitro and relies on NF-κB activation.
evidence: This is inferred from NF-κB inhibition experiments shown in Figure 5d.

claim: The poorly functional and altered structural organization of the vascular bed has an important impact on tumor progression and affects endothelial–leukocyte interactions.
source: The poorly functional and altered structural organization of the vascular bed has an important impact on tumor progression and affects endothelial–leukocyte interactions (Cedervall et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cedervall et al., 2015.

claim: CD3-RORγt+ ILCs are present in low-grade transitional bladder carcinoma in close proximity to CD31+ blood vessels.
source: First, we observed that CD3-RORγt+ ILCs are present in low-grade transitional bladder carcinoma in close proximity to CD31+ blood vessels (Figure 6a, panels 1–4)
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6a, panels 1–4.

claim: CD3-RORγt+ ILCs are barely detected in high-grade bladder carcinoma.
source: First, we observed that CD3-RORγt+ ILCs are present in low-grade transitional bladder carcinoma in close proximity to CD31+ blood vessels (Figure 6a, panels 1–4) but are barely detected in high-grade bladder carcinoma (Figure 6a, panels 5–8)
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6a, panels 5–8.

claim: The presence of RORγt-expressing ILCs in low-grade bladder carcinoma suggests a protective role at early stage of disease.
source: First, we observed that CD3-RORγt+ ILCs are present in low-grade transitional bladder carcinoma in close proximity to CD31+ blood vessels (Figure 6a, panels 1–4) but are barely detected in high-grade bladder carcinoma (Figure 6a, panels 5–8), suggesting a protective role of RORγt-expressing ILCs, at least at early stage of disease.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the differential presence of RORγt+ ILCs in low vs high-grade tumors.

claim: ILCPs are expanded in the PB of non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC) patients.
source: Interestingly, since we also observed that ILCPs are expanded in the PB of non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC) patients, but reduced in muscle-invasive stage of the disease (MIBC, Figure 6b)
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: ILCPs are reduced in the PB of muscle-invasive bladder cancer (MIBC) patients.
source: Interestingly, since we also observed that ILCPs are expanded in the PB of non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC) patients, but reduced in muscle-invasive stage of the disease (MIBC, Figure 6b)
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: The presence of ILCPs in NMIBC patients might underline the attempt of this cell population to support the infiltration of immune cells into the tumor site.
source: Interestingly, since we also observed that ILCPs are expanded in the PB of non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC) patients, but reduced in muscle-invasive stage of the disease (MIBC, Figure 6b), and, following in vitro expansion, ILCPs acquire RORγt expression, we hypothesized that the presence of ILCPs in NMIBC patients might underline the attempt of this cell population to support the infiltration of immune cells into the tumor site.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on ILCP distribution in patients and their EC-activating capacity.

claim: The capacity to upregulate adhesion molecule expression on ECs by ILCPs was significantly reduced after overnight incubation with bladder carcinoma cell lines, compared to resting ILCPs.
source: As shown in Figure 6c, the capacity to upregulate adhesion molecule expression on ECs by ILCPs was significantly reduced after the overnight incubation with bladder carcinoma cell lines, if compared to resting ILCPs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6c.

claim: The co-culture with MIBC lines showed the highest capacity to modify ILCP ability to activate the ECs.
source: Interestingly, the co-culture with MIBC lines showed the highest capacity to modify ILCP ability to activate the ECs (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is based on comparison of data in Figure 6c.

claim: Statistically significant reduced levels of IL-8, GM-CSF, and IFN-γ were observed when ECs were co-cultured with MIBC pre-exposed ILCPs.
source: Moreover, the analysis of the cytokine composition of the supernatants from 3 hr EC–ILCP co-culture revealed statistically significant reduced levels of the pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-8, GM-CSF, and IFN-γ when ECs where co-cultured with MIBC pre-exposed ILCPs (Figure 6d).
evidence: This is supported by cytokine measurement data shown in Figure 6d.

claim: TCC-Sup did not express IDO-1.
source: As shown in Figure 6e, TCC-Sup did not express IDO-1, suggesting that the tumor-mediated effects on ILCPs might not depend on kynurenines.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6e.

claim: The tumor-mediated effects on ILCPs might not depend on kynurenines.
source: As shown in Figure 6e, TCC-Sup did not express IDO-1, suggesting that the tumor-mediated effects on ILCPs might not depend on kynurenines.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of IDO-1 expression in TCC-Sup cells shown in Figure 6e.

claim: Following overnight incubation with ILCPs, TCC-Sup strongly upregulated CD39 and further increased CD73 expression.
source: However, following the overnight incubation with ILCPs, TCC-Sup strongly upregulated CD39 and further increased the CD73 expression (Figure 6e).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6e.

claim: Steady-state ILCPs expressed CD39, but very low levels of CD73.
source: Interestingly, steady-state ILCPs also expressed CD39, but very low levels of CD73 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1c)
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1c.

claim: In the presence of CD73+ cells, ILCPs might process ATP and support adenosine production.
source: Interestingly, steady-state ILCPs also expressed CD39, but very low levels of CD73 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1c), suggesting that, in the presence of CD73+ cells, ILCPs might process ATP and support adenosine production.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the expression of CD39 on ILCPs and CD73 on tumor cells.

claim: In vitro-expanded ILCPs upregulated the expression of A2A, A2B, and A3 adenosine receptors.
source: Interestingly, as shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1d, in vitro-expanded ILCPs upregulated the expression of A2A, A2B, and A3 receptors.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1d.

claim: Pre-exposure of ILCPs to 2-Chloroadenosine (a stabilized form of adenosine) reduced their EC-activating capacity.
source: Of note, pre-exposure of ILCPs to 2-Chloroadenosine (a stabilized form of adenosine) reduced their EC-activating capacity (Figure 6f).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6f.

claim: Tumor cells might impair or deviate, at least in part via adenosine production, the capacity of ILCs to modulate vascular activation through the upregulation of cell surface adhesion molecules.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that tumor cells might impair or deviate, at least in part via adenosine production, the capacity of ILCs to modulate vascular activation through the upregulation of cell surface adhesion molecules, and affect the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines upon EC–ILCP encounter.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data on CD39/CD73 expression, adenosine receptor expression, and 2-Chloroadenosine experiments.

claim: Tumor cells affect the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines upon EC–ILCP encounter.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that tumor cells might impair or deviate, at least in part via adenosine production, the capacity of ILCs to modulate vascular activation through the upregulation of cell surface adhesion molecules, and affect the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines upon EC–ILCP encounter.
evidence: This is supported by cytokine data shown in Figure 6d.

claim: Tumor impairment of ILCP function could represent a mechanism through which tumors can prevent and block immune cell infiltration into the tumor site.
source: Therefore, this could represent a mechanism through which tumors can prevent and block immune cell infiltration into the tumor site.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observed tumor-mediated impairment of ILCP EC-activating capacity.

claim: Group 3 ILCs (defined as Lin- CD127+NKp44+ cells) induce the expression of ICAM-1 and VCAM-1 on mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) after 4-day co-culture in the presence of IL-7.
source: Our results are consistent with previously reported data showing that group 3 ILCs (defined as Lin- CD127+NKp44+ cells) induce the expression of ICAM-1 and VCAM-1 on mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) after 4-day co-culture and in the presence of IL-7 (Cupedo et al., 2009; Crellin et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cupedo et al., 2009 and Crellin et al., 2010.

claim: Circulating ILCPs constitute a distinct subset from ILC3s, although they share the expression of c-Kit on their cell surface and are CRTH2−.
source: According to recent findings, circulating ILCPs constitute a distinct subset from ILC3s, although they share the expression of c-Kit on their cell surface and are CRTH2− (Lim et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lim et al., 2017.

claim: The upregulation of RORγt and the expression of activation markers argue for a conversion of ILCPs into committed ILC3-like cells following in vitro priming.
source: Following in vitro priming, the upregulation of RORγt and the expression of activation markers argue for a conversion of ILCPs into committed ILC3-like cells, possibly supported by IL-1β and/or other factors secreted by feeder cells during the expansion phase.
evidence: This is inferred from phenotypic data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c and d.

claim: The conversion of ILCPs into committed ILC3-like cells is possibly supported by IL-1β and/or other factors secreted by feeder cells during the expansion phase.
source: Following in vitro priming, the upregulation of RORγt and the expression of activation markers argue for a conversion of ILCPs into committed ILC3-like cells, possibly supported by IL-1β and/or other factors secreted by feeder cells during the expansion phase.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the culture conditions and observed phenotypic changes.

claim: The in vitro expansion environment mimics the in vivo dynamics observed during inflammatory processes driven by PAMP/DAMP/tumor-dependent DC activation.
source: This environment mimics the in vivo dynamics observed during inflammatory processes driven by PAMP/DAMP/tumor-dependent DC activation.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the biological relevance of the in vitro culture system.

claim: The in vitro culture of ILCPs isolated from the PB of HDs did not lead to the expansion of ILC1s or ILC2s, whereas only ILC3-like cells arose.
source: However, differently from what was described by Lim and colleagues (Lim et al., 2017), the in vitro culture of ILCPs isolated from the PB of HDs did not lead to the expansion of neither ILC1s nor ILC2s, whereas only ILC3-like cells arose.
evidence: This is based on observation from the in vitro expansion experiments and contrasts with findings from Lim et al., 2017.

claim: The in vitro stimulation applied in the current study differs from Lim et al.'s protocol, with the lack of ILC1-, ILC2-, or ILC3-specific cytokines.
source: Indeed, the in vitro stimulation applied in that context differs from our in vitro expansion protocol, with the lack of ILC1-, ILC2-, or ILC3-specific cytokines.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological difference between studies.

claim: The in vitro expansion of circulating ILCPs in the presence of feeder cells, PHA, and IL-2 favors their commitment toward an ILC3-like phenotype.
source: Overall, our findings support the idea that the in vitro expansion of circulating ILCPs in the presence of feeder cells, PHA, and IL-2 favors their commitment toward an ILC3-like phenotype.
evidence: This is inferred from the phenotypic and functional data presented in the study.

claim: Freshly isolated CD4+ CD45RO+ lymphocytes are able to induce, to different extents, the expression of VCAM-1 on ECs in a contact-dependent manner.
source: Interestingly, as far as adaptive immune cells are concerned, a previous publication showed that freshly isolated CD4+ CD45RO+ lymphocytes are able to induce, to different extents, the expression of VCAM-1 on ECs in a contact-dependent manner (Yarwood et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yarwood et al., 2000.

claim: The human NK cell line NK92 induces the expression of E-selectin and IL-8 in ECs through the LT-dependent activation of the NF-κB pathway.
source: For the innate counterpart, it was shown that the human NK cell line NK92 induces the expression of E-selectin and IL-8 in ECs, which results in EC activation, through the LT-dependent activation of the NF-κB pathway (von Albertini et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to von Albertini et al., 1998.

claim: In vitro-expanded purified primary NK cells did not upregulate adhesion molecules on ECs in the current study.
source: Yet, in our system, we did not observe the upregulation of adhesion molecules when employing in vitro-expanded purified primary NK cells (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated based on experimental observation (data not shown).

claim: Pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-8, GM-CSF, IFN-γ, and TNF) produced during the EC–ILCP interaction might contribute to the observed EC activation.
source: In this work, we define the ILCP-mediated activation of ECs primarily as a contact-dependent mechanism. However, we cannot exclude that pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-8, GM-CSF, IFN-γ, and TNF), produced during the EC–ILCP interaction, might contribute to the observed EC activation.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning acknowledging the potential contribution of soluble factors.

claim: Pro-inflammatory cytokines, especially TNF, constitute potent inducers of adhesion molecule expression in ECs.
source: It is known that pro-inflammatory cytokines, and especially TNF, constitute potent inducers of adhesion molecule expression in ECs (Collins et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Collins et al., 1995.

claim: ECs upregulate adhesion molecules expression only when short-term exposed to TNF, but not to other cytokines.
source: However, in our hands, ECs upregulate adhesion molecules expression only when short-term exposed to TNF, but not to the other cytokines (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated based on experimental observation (data not shown).

claim: The pro-inflammatory cytokines produced during the co-culture can support, at the cell–cell contact region, the in vitro cross-talk.
source: However, it cannot be excluded that the pro-inflammatory cytokines that are produced during the co-culture can support, at the cell–cell contact region, the in vitro cross-talk.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the potential local effects of cytokines at the cell-cell interface.

claim: RANKL has been recently described as a negative regulator of CCR6+ ILC3s activation and cytokine production, via the paracrine interaction with its receptor RANK.
source: RANKL has been recently described as a negative regulator of CCR6+ ILC3s activation and cytokine production, via the paracrine interaction with its receptor RANK (Bando et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bando et al., 2018.

claim: The expression of RANK on ex vivo ILCPs was not detectable.
source: On one side, we observed that the expression of RANK on ex vivo ILCPs was not detectable, whereas in vitro-expanded ILCPs acquire transient, intermediate levels of RANK after expansion (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated based on experimental observation (data not shown).

claim: In vitro-expanded ILCPs acquire transient, intermediate levels of RANK after expansion.
source: On one side, we observed that the expression of RANK on ex vivo ILCPs was not detectable, whereas in vitro-expanded ILCPs acquire transient, intermediate levels of RANK after expansion (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated based on experimental observation (data not shown).

claim: Very low levels of soluble TNF were observed at the end of the ILCP expansion.
source: Of note, we observed higher levels of transcripts in in vitro-expanded ILCPs compared to their ex vivo counterparts, but very low levels of soluble TNF at the end of the expansion, suggesting that TNF might be present on the surface of expanded ILCPs.
evidence: This is based on cytokine measurement data.

claim: TNF might be present on the surface of expanded ILCPs.
source: Of note, we observed higher levels of transcripts in in vitro-expanded ILCPs compared to their ex vivo counterparts, but very low levels of soluble TNF at the end of the expansion, suggesting that TNF might be present on the surface of expanded ILCPs.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on high TNF transcripts but low soluble TNF.

claim: A sequential engagement of TNF/TNFR and RANKL/RANK interactions might occur in the EC–ILCP interface.
source: We might speculate that a sequential engagement of these ligand–receptor interactions occurs in the EC–ILCP interface, with initial tm-TNF/TNFR interactions that are needed to induce adhesion molecules expression, together with increased RANK expression in ECs.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the combined blocking experiments and receptor expression data.

claim: Initial tm-TNF/TNFR interactions are needed to induce adhesion molecules expression and increase RANK expression in ECs.
source: We might speculate that a sequential engagement of these ligand–receptor interactions occurs in the EC–ILCP interface, with initial tm-TNF/TNFR interactions that are needed to induce adhesion molecules expression, together with increased RANK expression in ECs.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observed upregulation of RANK on ECs after ILCP exposure (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).

claim: Sequential RANKL/RANK interactions are possibly required to support the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines.
source: This could facilitate the sequential RANKL/RANK interactions, possibly required to support the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines, since the prevention of both TNFR/RANK engagement resulted in impaired cytokine production.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the cytokine data from combined blocking experiments (Figure 4—figure supplement 1e).

claim: ILCPs might favor the initial tethering of circulating immune cells to vascular ECs via E-Selectin induction.
source: Therefore, ILCPs might favor the initial tethering of circulating immune cells to vascular ECs via E-Selectin induction, and the subsequent ICAM-1/LFA-1 and VCAM-1/VLA-4-mediated firm adhesion step, and support the EC-dependent recruitment of other immune cell types, thus facilitating their exit from the blood stream through the vessel wall.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the functional adhesion assay data and known roles of adhesion molecules.

claim: ILCPs support the subsequent ICAM-1/LFA-1 and VCAM-1/VLA-4-mediated firm adhesion step.
source: Therefore, ILCPs might favor the initial tethering of circulating immune cells to vascular ECs via E-Selectin induction, and the subsequent ICAM-1/LFA-1 and VCAM-1/VLA-4-mediated firm adhesion step, and support the EC-dependent recruitment of other immune cell types, thus facilitating their exit from the blood stream through the vessel wall.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the functional adhesion assay data and known roles of adhesion molecules.

claim: ILCPs support the EC-dependent recruitment of other immune cell types, facilitating their exit from the blood stream through the vessel wall.
source: Therefore, ILCPs might favor the initial tethering of circulating immune cells to vascular ECs via E-Selectin induction, and the subsequent ICAM-1/LFA-1 and VCAM-1/VLA-4-mediated firm adhesion step, and support the EC-dependent recruitment of other immune cell types, thus facilitating their exit from the blood stream through the vessel wall.

claim: NKp46+ ILCs were crucial for the establishment of an IL-12-dependent anti-tumor immune response in a subcutaneous melanoma mouse model.
source: As previously reported (Eisenring et al., 2010), NKp46+ ILCs were described to be crucial, in a subcutaneous melanoma mouse model, for the establishment of an IL-12-dependent anti-tumor immune response.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Eisenring et al., 2010.

claim: A similar role to NKp46+ ILCs was proposed for NKp44+ ILC3s in NSCLC patients.
source: A similar role was proposed for NKp44+ ILC3s in NSCLC patients (Carrega et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Carrega et al., 2015.

claim: NKp44+ ILC3s' role in supporting intratumoral TLS formation has been further recently supported in colorectal cancer patients.
source: Beside their putative role in supporting intratumoral TLS formation, an aspect that has been further recently supported in colorectal cancer patients (Ikeda et al., 2020)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ikeda et al., 2020.

claim: NKp44+ ILC3s were suggested to activate tumor-associated ECs and favor leukocyte recruitment.
source: Beside their putative role in supporting intratumoral TLS formation, an aspect that has been further recently supported in colorectal cancer patients (Ikeda et al., 2020), these cells were suggested to activate tumor-associated ECs and, in turn, favor leukocyte recruitment.
evidence: This is stated as a suggested mechanism based on previous literature.

source: Hence, ILCP–EC interactions might represent an early event during a large spectrum of biological reactions, ranging from inflammation, autoimmunity, and cancer.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the broader biological significance of the findings.

evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about leukocyte trafficking in tumors.

source: The infiltration of immune cells in solid tumors often correlates with a better overall survival in cancer patients (Zhang et al., 2003, Tjin and Luiten, 2014, Mina et al., 2015).

source: However, in the tumor microenvironment, ECs are dysfunctional and play a major role in several processes that contribute to cancer-associated mortality.

claim: ETBR signaling in tumor ECs was responsible for the impaired ICAM-1-dependent T cell homing to tumors and correlated with shorter patient survival.
source: By transcriptionally profiling the tumor ECs (TECs) isolated from ovarian cancer specimens poorly infiltrated by T cells, the authors describe a mechanism that relies on the interaction between endothelin B receptor (ETBR), found to be highly expressed by TECs, and its ligand endothelin-1 (ET-1), overexpressed in ovarian cancer cells. ETBR signaling was shown to be responsible for the impaired ICAM-1-dependent T cell homing to tumors, and in turn, it correlated with shorter patient survival.
evidence: This is based on the work by Buckanovich et al., 2008 as described in the text.

claim: Overexpression of Fas ligand (FasL) on TEC surface prevents T cell infiltration into tumors by causing selective killing of tumor-specific CD8+ T cells and accumulation of FoxP3+ T regulatory cells.
source: Another mechanism that prevents T cell infiltration into the tumors relies on the overexpression of Fas ligand (FasL) on TEC surface (Motz et al., 2014) that causes the selective killing of tumor-specific CD8+ T cells and to the accumulation of FoxP3+ T regulatory (Tregs) cells within the tumors.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Motz et al., 2014.

claim: The shaping of an immunosuppressive milieu together with the diversion of the vascular system supports tumor progression and favors metastatic dissemination.
source: The shaping of an immunosuppressive milieu together with the diversion of the vascular system supports tumor progression and favors metastatic dissemination (Hida and Maishi, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hida and Maishi, 2018.

claim: RORγt-expressing ILCs infiltrate both human low-grade bladder and colon cancers and are associated with CD31+ vessels.
source: Here we show that RORγt-expressing ILCs, which share the transcription factor with in vitro-expanded ILCPs, infiltrate both human low-grade bladder and colon cancers and are associated with CD31+ vessels, arguing for a potential ILC–EC interaction also in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6a and Figure 6—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The association of RORγt-expressing ILCs with CD31+ vessels argues for a potential ILC–EC interaction in vivo.
source: Here we show that RORγt-expressing ILCs, which share the transcription factor with in vitro-expanded ILCPs, infiltrate both human low-grade bladder and colon cancers and are associated with CD31+ vessels, arguing for a potential ILC–EC interaction also in vivo.

claim: ILCs are very plastic cells.
source: ILCs are very plastic cells (Bal et al., 2020)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bal et al., 2020.

claim: Tumor-derived TGF-β drives the transition of NK cells to dysfunctional and pro-tumoral ILC1s in vivo.
source: ILCs are very plastic cells (Bal et al., 2020), and it has been reported that, in the cancer setting, tumor-derived TGF-β drives the transition of NK cells to dysfunctional and pro-tumoral ILC1s in vivo, a novel mechanism exploited by tumors to prevent the establishment of an innate anti-tumor response (Gao et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gao et al., 2017.

claim: Tumor-derived TGF-β-mediated conversion of NK cells to ILC1s is a novel mechanism exploited by tumors to prevent the establishment of an innate anti-tumor response.
source: ILCs are very plastic cells (Bal et al., 2020), and it has been reported that, in the cancer setting, tumor-derived TGF-β drives the transition of NK cells to dysfunctional and pro-tumoral ILC1s in vivo, a novel mechanism exploited by tumors to prevent the establishment of an innate anti-tumor response (Gao et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gao et al., 2017.

claim: A similar conversion to that observed for NK cells might also occur for ILCPs toward a non-EC activating ILC subset.
source: One can speculate that a similar conversion also occurs for ILCPs toward a non-EC activating ILC subset.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observed tumor-mediated impairment of ILCPs and known ILC plasticity.

source: The presence of these two ectoenzymes, key for adenosine production, suggest that adenosine might be produced during the co-culture between cancer cells and ILCPs and impact ILCP functions.
evidence: This is inferred from the expression of CD39 and CD73 shown in Figure 6e and Figure 6—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Adenosine produced during cancer cell-ILCP co-culture might impact ILCP functions.
source: The presence of these two ectoenzymes, key for adenosine production, suggest that adenosine might be produced during the co-culture between cancer cells and ILCPs and impact ILCP functions.

claim: ILCPs, upon proper stimulation, might represent novel players in regulating the trafficking of immune cells to tissues during the early phase of inflammation and at early phases of anti-tumor immune responses.
source: In conclusion, our data show that ILCPs, upon proper stimulation, might represent novel players in regulating the trafficking of immune cells to tissues, not only during the early phase of inflammation, but also at early phases of anti-tumor immune responses.
evidence: This is a concluding statement that synthesizes the findings of the study.

source: Such contact-mediated events may be crucial in supporting further EC activation, to favor tumor-specific T-cell adhesion and, in turn, recruitment to the tumor site.
